catalog_quote: [Anderson 2008: 686] 2.5 Intonation / stress Stress occurs in final position in Gta ? words, with some exceptions . For example, some morphemic combinations attract stress ( the negative in combination with a second singular subject in various conjugations), while others disprefer it ( the tense / aspect suffixes) . Longer words have secondary stress patterns, but these also remain to be investigated . [Hildebrandt & Anderson 2023: 552] 17.3.5 Gtar ( Gta ?, southern Odisha, northern Andhra Pradesh) This same pattern also appears to characterize Gta ?: Prosodic words are maximally three syllables, with many grammatical elements in final position extrametrical, and these may take stress only when appearing with a monosyllabic stem . Four- syllable grammatical word sequences can sometimes divide into two prosodic words, each with their own stress pattern, but if the final two syllables are both grammatical elements, stress remains on the second syllable . Stress has not yet been studied instrumentally for Gta ?, but it impressionistically appears to fall on the second syllable . ( 44) Hill Gta ? new_statements.rule_in_words: Impressionistic, non-instrumental: primary stress falls at the right edge of the lexical word, i.e. on the final syllable of (mostly mono-/disyllabic, often sesquisyllabic) stems = the second syllable; inflectional material at the end (tense/aspect suffixes, clitic chains) is normally unstressed/extrametrical, so in longer grammatical words stress stays on the second syllable. The same author's later first-hand account (Hildebrandt & Anderson 2023: 552) words it as: prosodic words maximally three syllables, final grammatical elements extrametrical (stressable only after a monosyllabic stem), four-syllable sequences may split into two prosodic words, otherwise 'stress remains on the second syllable.. it impressionistically appears to fall on the second syllable'. 'Final' (2008) and 'second' (2023) coincide for the canonical disyllabic word; I read the pair as second-syllable/right-edge-of-stem stress, morphologically conditioned, not yet verified acoustically.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Anderson 2008: 'Longer words have secondary stress patterns, but these also remain to be investigated.' No rule given.
new_statements.exceptions: Some morpheme combinations attract stress (negative + 2sg subject in various conjugations); tense/aspect suffixes 'disprefer' stress (2008). 2023: final grammatical elements are extrametrical but may take stress when the stem is monosyllabic; four-syllable grammatical words can form two prosodic words each with its own stress.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level (phonological/prosodic word vs. grammatical word distinction made explicit in 2023). Both statements are impressionistic; Hildebrandt & Anderson 2023 and Horo & Anderson 2021 state that Gtaʔ stress has not been studied instrumentally. 2008 sketch is based mainly on Plains Gtaʔ; the 2023 stressed examples are Hill Gtaʔ.
new_statements.identity_note: Anderson 2008 describes mainly Plains Gtaʔ (data largely from Mahapatra & Zide's plains-village materials; 'Plains Gtaʔ and Hill Gtaʔ are the recognized varieties', p. 682); the stress-marked examples in Hildebrandt & Anderson 2023 (44) are labelled Hill Gtaʔ. Glottolog gata1239 is language-level and (to my knowledge) has no separate dialect codes for Plains vs Hill Gtaʔ. Vedamanickam 2002 'Didei' = the same language under the Odia exonym (Didayi/Didei), Plains variety, Malkangiri district.

sources.note: Diachronic/comparative only: p. 6 'Only in iambic words may Munda languages lose the vowel of the initial syllable, either just in allegro speech, as in Sora torib ~ trib, or generally, as in the Gtaʔ language'; p. 18 '(In Gtaʔ, the unaccented vowel was lost, and the accented *ə became /a/.)' citing DeArmond 1976. General claim (pp. 5-6) that Munda word accent is initial except in iambic words where it falls on the heavy second syllable (Sora-based). No synchronic Gtaʔ rule.
